pr_title: Make all interpolated string handlers pass by ref
pr_body:
We currently pass all of our interpolated string handlers to their destination methods by ref, with the exception of those for Debug.  I think it makes sense to centralize on the pattern of always passing by ref: it doesn’t negatively impact the user experience, these are typically larger structs and so by ref helps (though it doesn’t matter for Debug), making it a ref makes it even less attractive to try to call directly / makes it look even more special, and most importantly, it gives us the opportunity to more safely clean up at the end of the operation.  This changes the Debug.Assert/Write{Line}If overloads we added in Preview 7 to pass the handler’s by ref.

This also then updates the Debug.Write{Line}If methods to create the StringBuilder used via StringBuilderCache, just in case these are used in a scenario where true is frequently passed.  With the handler passed by ref, we can more correctly clean up.

cc: @bartonjs, @GrabYourPitchforks 
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/57526
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/57538

issue_context.title: Debug Diagnostics always allocates StringBuilder with new optimized String Interpolation
issue_context.body:
When using the old string.Format then it would make use of internal StringBuilder-pool.

Now it always allocates a new StringBuilder, and throws it away:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/dfd618dc648ba9b11dd0f8034f78113d69f223cd/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Diagnostics/Debug.cs#L301

Issue Details
When using the old string.Format then it would make use of internal StringBuilder-pool. Now it always allocates a new StringBuilder, and throws it away: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/dfd618dc648ba9b11dd0f8034f78113d69f223cd/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Diagnostics/Debug.cs#L301
Author: snakefoot
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Diagnostics`, `untriaged`
Milestone: -

That code is not for string.Format. That's the code for Debug.Assert, which is only compiled in for `#define DEBUG`, and specifically on the path where Debug.Assert is given a false condition, which means it's failing an assert and by default is about to crash the process.  Why is a `StringBuilder` allocation there concerning?

Lets try again old-style-interpolated-strings would convert into string.Format, and string.Format would make use of StringBuilder-pool.

Also it is not only `Debug.Assert` that have received additional springles. The same also applies for `Debug.WriteIf` and `Debug.WriteLineIf` that hopefully doesn't crash the process.

Why not use `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler` instead of `StringBuilder.AppendInterpolatedStringHandler` in `Debug` ?

> Why not use DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler instead of StringBuilder.AppendInterpolatedStringHandler in Debug ?

Because DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler is a ref struct.

> The same also applies for Debug.WriteIf and Debug.WriteLineIf that hopefully doesn't crash the process.

Yes, they will allocate a StringBuilder if `#if DEBUG` is set and the condition dictates they should write a message, which is typically a rare occurrence for which an extra StringBuilder won't matter.  It does not seem like a good tradeoff to either a) duplicate a lot of code to avoid that or b) make this a ref struct and thereby limit how it can be used (e.g. awaits in format holes).

Just strange that it is promoted as a performance improvement with less-allocation, but then becomes a knife in your back (when the condition is true)

Anyway I just looked for some example code of how to use the new optimization, but I guess I have to continue looking (Yes it is a little annoying everyone have to carbon-copy `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler` to make their own correct handler)

> becomes a knife in your back (when the condition is true)

Can you please share concrete examples of where you're using Debug.WriteIf(true, $"...") on code paths where the extra StringBuilder matters?

If they exist,  it's fixable with more code.  It simply seems to me right now like the wrong tradeoff to add more code for this.

Thanks.

I think it makes good sense for `Debug.Assert()`. I was just curious why this decision was made for `Debug.WriteIf` (And now you have told that it is because `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler` is impossible to reuse).

Now I just have to figure out why Microsoft have implemented an optimization, that only can be used for Logging just before crashing the process (And hard to reuse anywhere else without inferring a performance hit because of StringBuilder-allocations).

> Now I just have to figure out why Microsoft have implemented an optimization, that only can be used for Logging just before crashing the process (And hard to reuse anywhere else without inferring a performance hit because of StringBuilder-allocations).

Huh? I don't understand your question / comment.

> Huh? I don't understand your question / comment.

Lets say I have another place where I want to check a condition, before doing the string-interpolation (Just like `Debug.WriteIf`)

How would I do that, since I cannot use `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler` ? And I don't want to use `AppendInterpolatedStringHandler` because of the StringBuilder-allocation-hit ?
Pool StringBuilders, or implement appends yourself using whatever mechanism you want, or create your handler as a ref struct, or...

Yep thank you for confirming that implementing own StringBuilder-pool is only way forward. Maybe update the [The handler pattern](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/proposals/csharp-10.0/improved-interpolated-strings#the-handler-pattern) with concrete example that uses `AppendInterpolatedStringHandler` with a note about optional StringBuilder-pool (To avoid higher allocation rate than old string-format).

And also explain that `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler` cannot be wrapped in a custom-handler because it is very sensitive about its lifetime (`ref struct`).

> implementing own StringBuilder-pool is only way forward

It is not the only way. 

But thank you for the feedback.

> It is not the only way.

So how to I get a the formatted-string using a custom-handler without allocating the StringBuilder, and not doing carbon-copy of `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler`?
Make your handler a ref struct.
Why did you not decide not to make `AssertInterpolatedStringHandler` a `ref struct` and re-use `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler` ?
Based on the stated belief that allocations in those situations do not matter.
Thank you for the answers. Though I still don't understand the choice to opt-in for allocations, when it is just a matter of changing to `ref struct` to fix it. But I have what I need.

> I still don't understand the choice to opt-in for allocations, when it is just a matter of changing to ref struct to fix it

If a handler is a ref struct, you can't do `$"...{await Foo()}..."` with awaits _inside_ of formatting holes.  In our experience, that's a very rare need, but technically it is a functional limitation.  So you trade that off against other costs.  If you believe that additional overhead isn't a big deal when passing true to Debug.WriteIf, because that's typically only done in debug builds when you're gathering additional information about something that's not working correctly, then it's better to accomodate even that rare need than to avoid costs that don't matter.  If you believe that those costs do matter in these situations, then you make a different tradeoff, e.g. adding additional code to implement appending yourself, or pooling StringBuilders to use the existing logic there, and so on.
